name: Yara Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Bramble & Co, five of us in a converted barn just outside town. Our clients are family businesses: farm shops, a honey producer, a tyre garage, a couple of cafés. I do their logos, labels, posters and the posts they put online, and I'm the one who looks after the AI side. What I love is when a family business gets busier because of something I made. What wears me out is the endless little resizes, though AI does most of those now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the AI side.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I brought it in, honestly, after watching videos at night. Helen Bramble, who owns the agency, was nervous, but once she saw me turn a label into twelve versions in ten minutes she was sold. The market doesn't care how hard you worked at university. It cares what you can do this year, so I keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and leave it there. At work I'd keep showing Helen new tricks. Online I'd probably post a few tips, because people find that useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me. A farm shop owner doesn't want a robot. The owner wants someone who'll pick up the phone on a Sunday when the honey labels print wrong. I've got about five months saved, and our clients are loyal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools every day to get through the routine work faster. I'd do more for my parents' corner shop, their signs and their online posts, for free, because family's family. And I'd start putting a bit into a savings account for a deposit with Karim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe slightly disappointed it wasn't bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' shop. The big supermarket opened on the ring road last year and they've felt it. That worries me more than anything about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your parents' shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Run their offers online, make the shop look sharper, maybe set up deliveries for the older customers. I can't fix the supermarket, but I can help them fight back.

say: AI is a **useful tool**, nothing bigger.
I'd post a few **tips online** and keep showing Helen new tricks.
think: Clients are **loyal**, and I've got about **five months** saved.
Small businesses want **a real person** on the phone, not a robot.
do: Keep using the **tools daily** for routine resizes and labels.
Do **free design work** for my parents' corner shop.
Start **saving for a deposit** with Karim.
feel: **Calm**, and slightly disappointed it wasn't bigger.

fieldNote: She's **secure** in this world: loyal clients, healthy savings, strong tool skills.

**Family** is central; she helps her parents unpaid without a second thought.

steps.text: Keep using AI daily for label and poster resizes
Open a deposit savings account with Karim
Redo signs and online offers for her parents' corner shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how markets work, and the people who adapt do well. At work I'd tell everyone to learn the tools now. I'd say it online too, but politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a bit strange. I brought the AI tools into Bramble & Co myself. I'd be lying if I said I never thought about building the thing that replaces me. But I think I'm the one at Bramble & Co who stays, because I'm the one who runs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Helen to let me set up the automated label and post system for all our clients, and charge them a monthly fee for it. I'd ask for a share in the business in return, even a small one. And I'd keep saving, because Karim's accountancy work is on the same list on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm fine, but I'm watching Karim and the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karim. His firm's already using software for the routine bookkeeping. If they stop hiring juniors, he's next in the queue to be squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the government involved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd want government to stay out of it, mostly. If anything, help with apprenticeships and let families sort out the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, now, because waiting won't help. At work I'd tell Helen we need a plan for the next twelve months. Online I'd say look to your family and your local community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, here's the thing. My partner Karim is an accountant and I'm a designer. In a two-year AGI world, that's two desk jobs under one roof, and that frightens me. I think my design job lasts maybe a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my parents and talk about me joining the shop, because shop work is hands-on and the robots come about three years later, around 2031. I'd sell the AI setups to other agencies while that's still worth something. Karim and I would stop saving for a deposit and keep the cash in case one of us loses our job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first time in this conversation I've felt properly worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's always wanted me in the shop, and I always said no, I've got a degree. He'd probably be smug. But I'd be grateful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the year before it lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell anything that's tool-related while it's still in demand, like the setups and training. Then I'd put that money into the shop, maybe deliveries or a café corner.

Look to **family and community**, which is what I'd say online.
think: My design job lasts **maybe a year**.

Karim's **accountancy** work would go on the same date as mine.

feel: **Alarmed**, for the first time in the conversation.
S2.quote: My partner Karim is an accountant and I'm a designer. In a two-year AGI world, that's two desk jobs under one roof, and that frightens me.
fieldNote: She's alarmed less for herself than for the **household**: two desk jobs at risk.
Her fallback is the **family shop**, which she once refused.
Free-market and adaptive, she'd **cash in** her tool skills fast.

steps.text: Join her parents' corner shop within the year
Sell AI label setups to other small agencies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift, so plan. At work I'd tell Helen we could become the agency that runs AI for family businesses. Online I'd share what's working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I've got a few good years and then design stops being a job. My parents' corner shop paid for my degree. In five years, I might be the one keeping that shop alive. That's not a bad thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own small studio on the side this year, doing AI-run labels and posts for family businesses, with Helen's blessing. I'd put some of my savings into the shop, a delivery van or a café corner. By year four I'd want the shop and my studio running together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I like having something to work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Karim?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karim does the books for the shop and my studio for a few years. After that, I don't know. He'd need to retrain into something hands-on too, or come into the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. My parents are getting older. If I'm in the shop, I'm nearby when they need me.

Bramble & Co could **run AI** for family businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. At work I'd say let's grow while we can. Online I'd encourage people to start learning things now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's a good version for me. Nobody owes me a career. Ten years is enough time to build my own studio, and if that goes too, I'll build something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Bramble & Co for two or three years and learn everything about running an agency. Then I'd go out on my own with family-business clients. Karim and I would buy a small house and maybe start a family around thirty-two. I'd put a little into an index fund each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. There's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a family in that timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in about five years. I'd want my studio running first so I can work from home when the kids are small. That's the plan I'd want even without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens with your parents' shop then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help them, probably by modernising the shop and finding someone to run it day to day. But in ten years, it's my parents' decision, not mine.

steps.text: Go solo serving family businesses after three years at Bramble

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because Karim and I would both be in trouble at once and there'd be no time to set anything up. What would help is cheap business loans for family firms and apprenticeships, not handouts. And honestly, families looking after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I think it's fair. I don't think fair comes into it. It's the market, and you either move with it or it moves past you.

headlineQuote: The market doesn't care how hard you worked at university. It cares what you can do this year, so I keep learning.
portrait: Yara is a 27-year-old designer at **Bramble & Co**, doing labels, logos and posts for family businesses.
She uses AI **every day** and brought the tools into the agency herself.
Her partner **Karim** is an accountant, so two desk jobs share one household.
Her backstop is her **parents' corner shop**, which she once refused to work in.
She's calm in the mild worlds, **alarmed** in the fast one, and hopeful with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Karim would both lose desk jobs at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap business loans** for family firms and apprenticeships, not handouts.
